title: Truth, not eloquence (I.5)
hook: two printouts at a wedding lectern, one grand and one plain: chapter five says seek truth in scripture, not fine words
tomorrow: why would anyone say taking advice is safer than giving it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rumor and a hovering thumb: don't believe every word, and don't rush to pass it on. The line was weigh it.
screen: `DON'T BELIEVE IT, DON'T PASS IT ON.` → `WEIGH IT.`

segments.voice: A cousin is asked to read at a wedding. At the lectern she has two printouts of the same passage. One is full of thee and thou and long rolling sentences. The other reads like a text from a friend. Her hands are shaking a little. Which one is more true? Chapter five of The Imitation of Christ would tell her the question is a good one, and the answer isn't about sound at all.
screen: `TWO PRINTOUTS, ONE PASSAGE.` → `GRAND OR PLAIN?` → `WHICH ONE IS MORE TRUE?`

segments.voice: Truth, not eloquence, is what to look for in holy scripture, the chapter says. Read it for what it gives you, not for fine phrasing. Read simple, devout books as gladly as lofty ones. And then the line worth repeating to a friend tonight: don't ask who said it; mark what is said. Don't be swayed by a writer's reputation, great learning or small. Let love of plain truth draw you to read. Why? Because people pass away, but, quoting a psalm, as the Douay-Rheims puts it: "the truth of the Lord remaineth for ever." God speaks in many ways, the chapter says, and without favoring anyone. Then a gentle warning about ourselves. Curiosity often gets in the way, it says, when we try to pick apart and argue over what we should simply take in and move past. So the counsel is three plain words: read humbly, simply, faithfully. And don't wish to be known as learned. That loops back to chapter two, love to be unknown. For the cousin at the lectern, the grand version and the plain one can carry the same truth. What matters is that the people listening can hear it.
screen: `TRUTH, NOT ELOQUENCE.` · `MARK WHAT IS SAID, NOT WHO.` · `THE TRUTH OF THE LORD REMAINETH.` · `HUMBLY, SIMPLY, FAITHFULLY.` · then, large: `TRUTH, NOT STYLE.`

segments.voice: Say one short line aloud, plainly, no performance voice, the way you'd tell a friend something true. The psalm's line works: the truth of the Lord remaineth for ever. Say it once more, slower, and let the plain words stay with you.
Truth. What chapter five says to seek in scripture: not fine words, not famous names, but what is said.
Keep this one: truth, not style, whether the words come grand or plain. Talk tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1468 COUNTS.` → `THE IMITATION · 7 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: WHY WOULD ANYONE SAY TAKING ADVICE IS SAFER THAN GIVING IT?`

howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics hear scripture read aloud from the Lectionary in a translation the Church approves; at home, some read whichever faithful translation they understand, slowly, for what it says.

chat.says: writing my letter to oregon's coach. dad says sound impressive, mia says just be honest. who's right?
options: Mia, mostly. The Imitation says seek truth, not fine words: what's said matters most.
Your dad. Truth lands better in impressive words, so polish every line first.
Neither. Coaches don't really read letters, so it doesn't matter what you say.
chat.meaning: Chapter five says seek truth, not eloquence, and mark what is said. Plain words can carry the truth.

The Imitation of Christ.meaning: a short book of counsel credited to Thomas à Kempis

eloquence.meaning: fine, polished, persuasive speaking or writing

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an old Catholic English Bible translation

lectern.meaning: the stand a reader uses to read aloud in church

sources.work: The Imitation of Christ (attributed to Thomas à Kempis)

notes: Imitation I.5 paraphrased: truth, not eloquence, is to be sought in holy scripture; seek profit rather than subtlety of speech; read simple and devout books as willingly as high and profound ones; let not the authority of the writer offend you, whether of little or great learning, but let the love of pure truth draw you; inquire not who said it, but mark what is said; men pass away, but the truth of the Lord remains for ever; God speaks in divers manners without respect of persons; curiosity often hinders us; read humbly, simply and faithfully, and never desire the name of learned. Confirm.
Psalm 116:2 quoted from Douay-Rheims; the Imitation quotes it (Vulgate Ps 116:2). Confirm.
